Quantitative Research | Market Performance and Macroeconomic Relationships

Research report generated October 25, 2026 at 07:48 PM

Executive Summary

This project examines the historical performance of the semiconductor ETF SOXX relative to the broad-market ETF SPY, alongside changes in the effective federal funds rate. It combines market-price analysis, monthly macroeconomic data, and regression models.

The central question is whether changes in interest rates are associated with the semiconductor sector's relative performance after accounting for broad-market returns.

Main interpretation: The current simple regression results show a strong positive association between SPY monthly returns and SOXX monthly returns. The previous month's change in the effective federal funds rate is not statistically significant in this sample. These results do not establish causation.

The effective federal funds rate is not the same as a target-rate announcement or an unexpected monetary-policy shock.

Performance Statistics

These statistics are calculated from the available daily price data. Annualized volatility uses daily returns and a 252-trading-day convention. Maximum drawdown measures the largest peak-to-trough decline in the observed price series.

Regression Results

The main multivariable model estimates SOXX monthly returns using SPY monthly returns and the previous month's change in the effective federal funds rate.

The model uses heteroskedasticity-consistent HC3 standard errors. This adjustment helps address heteroskedasticity but does not automatically correct for every possible time-series issue.

Methodology

  1. Obtain historical daily prices for SOXX and SPY.
  2. Calculate daily returns, cumulative performance, annualized volatility, and drawdowns.
  3. Obtain the effective federal funds rate from FRED.
  4. Combine the market and macroeconomic datasets at a monthly frequency.
  5. Compare SOXX returns with SPY returns and changes in the rate series.
  6. Estimate regression models and report coefficients, uncertainty, and statistical significance.

Limitations and Interpretation

  • Association is not causation. A statistical relationship alone does not show that interest rates caused a change in semiconductor-stock performance.
  • Limited sample size. The multivariable monthly regression uses approximately 57 observations, so estimates may be sensitive to individual months.
  • Potential omitted variables. Earnings expectations, technology demand, inflation, market sentiment, and other macroeconomic factors can affect returns.
  • Timing and measurement. Monthly-average rates do not isolate the market reaction to individual policy announcements or unexpected rate decisions.
  • Time-series considerations. Serial correlation, changing relationships, and structural breaks may affect inference. HC3 standard errors alone do not resolve these issues.
  • Historical performance. Past returns and estimated relationships do not guarantee future performance.

Next Research Steps

  1. Test Newey-West/HAC standard errors for the monthly regression.
  2. Compare results across different sample periods.
  3. Test whether lagged market and rate variables improve the model.
  4. Consider additional macroeconomic variables and sector-specific controls.
  5. Evaluate out-of-sample performance before making any forecasting claims.
